modules.title: Deploy and manage applications using Microsoft Intune
modules.learnSummary: Plan and deploy applications across Windows devices using Microsoft Intune, including Microsoft Store, Microsoft 365, Win32, and line-of-business apps.
modules.tldr: Intune deploys Windows apps as Win32 (.intunewin), Microsoft Store, Windows Package Manager (WinGet), Microsoft 365 Apps or line-of-business packages, each with its own level of install and update control. You choose an assignment intent (Required, Available, Uninstall), target Entra ID groups refined by filters, and set user or system context. When something fails, you work from the admin center status down to the Intune Management Extension logs on the device.
objectives: Identify application deployment options in Microsoft Intune.
Plan an application deployment strategy that matches your app inventory.
Deploy Microsoft Store, Microsoft 365, Win32, and line-of-business apps using Intune.
Configure app availability, targeting, and install behavior.
Configure app update and assignment settings.
Monitor app deployments and troubleshoot installation failures.
keyPoints: **Win32 apps** give the most control: package with the Win32 Content Prep Tool into **.intunewin**, then add detection rules, return codes, requirements, dependencies and supersedence.
**Microsoft Store app (new)** uses **WinGet** and the Intune Management Extension; updates are automatic and **can't be scheduled or deferred** in Intune. Store for Business/Education is retired.
**Microsoft 365 Apps** are configured as a suite: pick apps, 32/64-bit, **update channel** (Current, Monthly Enterprise, Semi-Annual Enterprise) and languages.
Three assignment intents: **Required** (auto-install, kept installed, retried), **Available for enrolled devices** (Company Portal, user choice), **Uninstall** (removed at next sync).
**User-targeted** apps follow the user to every enrolled device; **device-targeted** apps install regardless of who signs in. **Assignment filters** refine groups by OS, ownership, model and more.
Removing a user from an assignment group **doesn't uninstall** the app — put them in an **Uninstall** assignment to remove it.
**Required assignments drive automatic updates**; with Available assignments you can't enforce a minimum version.
Troubleshoot from **Troubleshoot + support** to the IME logs in `C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\IntuneManagementExtension\Logs` — **AppWorkload.log** shows install steps and exit codes.

units.title: Understand application deployment options in Microsoft Intune
points: Each deployment combines an app type, an assignment intent, users or devices, and targeting via Entra ID groups and filters.
WinGet apps install common catalog apps (browsers, runtimes, dev tools) without a .intunewin package; use Win32 for custom apps or when you need detection rules, dependencies or return codes.
Store and WinGet apps both use WinGet infrastructure but different sources: Microsoft Store catalog vs. the Windows Package Manager community repository.
System context makes the app available to all users of the device; user context only to that user.
Win32 updates are delivered as a new package with supersedence of the older version.

units.title: Plan application deployment for your organization
points: Build an inventory, categorize apps by business criticality and identify app owners.
Map dependencies (.NET, Visual C++, Java), OS and hardware requirements, admin rights and licensing restrictions.
Decide whether to deploy as-is or repackage (add configuration, remove components, bundle dependencies).
Pilot and run UAT, then roll out in phases: pilot users → pilot departments → broader organization.
Stagger large deployments to off-hours or across groups to protect bandwidth.

units.title: Deploy Microsoft Store apps using Microsoft Intune
points: Add as **Microsoft Store app (new)**, search the Store catalog in the admin center, review metadata, choose install behavior, assign.
Free Store apps fit directly; paid apps go via Enterprise App Catalog, Win32 packaging or the publisher's volume licensing — not the retired Store for Business.
System context suits shared devices, kiosks and labs; on Entra registered devices System context is required. Avoid mixing contexts for the same app.
Devices need the Intune Management Extension and network access to Store, WinGet source and content endpoints.

units.title: Deploy Microsoft 365 apps using Microsoft Intune
points: Add via **Apps > All apps > Add > Windows > Microsoft 365 Apps for Windows 10 and later**, then configure the app suite.
Select only the apps a role needs, 32- or 64-bit, update channel and language packs.
Current Channel: new features up to three times a month; Monthly Enterprise: once a month; Semi-Annual Enterprise: every six months for maximum stability.
Requires Windows 10 or later and suitable Microsoft 365 licensing — Intune doesn't manage the licences.
You can remove older Office versions during install; individual updates can't be delayed, but you can switch channels.

units.title: Deploy Win32 apps using Microsoft Intune
points: Package .exe/.msi plus supporting files with the Win32 Content Prep Tool into a .intunewin file.
Configure install context, silent install/uninstall commands, requirement rules (e.g. architecture x64/x86/ARM64) and detection rules (file, registry, MSI product code — most reliable for MSI).
Return code 0 = success by default; map codes such as 3010 to restart-required handling so Intune doesn't retry.
Dependencies install first (max 100 incl. nested); supersedence replaces older versions (max 10 nodes in a chain).
Failures: check the IntuneManagementExtension logs on the device.

units.title: Deploy line-of-business (LOB) apps using Microsoft Intune
points: LOB apps are internal or exclusively purchased apps not in public stores.
Formats: Windows .msi, .appx/.appxbundle/.msix; iOS/iPadOS .ipa; Android .apk or managed Google Play; macOS .pkg.
MSIX is the most widely deployed modern format: background updates applied at next launch; MSI updates may need off-hours scheduling.
Upload a new version to replace the old one; check OS/architecture compatibility, dependencies, phased rollout and user communication.

units.title: Configure app availability, targeting, and install behavior
points: Required installs immediately, Available waits for the user, Uninstall removes the software.
User targeting follows the user across devices; device targeting fits kiosks and shared devices. Dynamic groups and filters reduce group sprawl.
Required installs are retried after failure; offline devices install once they check in again.
Removing a user from an assignment doesn't uninstall the app — use an Uninstall assignment and make sure the user isn't still in the old group.
Status: installed, pending, failed, or not applicable (device doesn't meet requirements such as minimum OS).

units.title: Configure app update and assignment settings
points: Store apps update through the Store; you can't schedule or delay them, and Intune can't confirm the device runs the latest Store version.
Win32 and LOB apps give the most update control, including staging updates to test groups.
Required assignments push new versions automatically; Available leaves updating to users; Uninstall overrides earlier Required/Available assignments for that group.
Use App Install Status, Device Install Status and Discovered Apps reports; example thresholds: investigate Required apps below 95% success, escalate below 85%.
At scale, use Endpoint analytics, Log Analytics workbooks, the Power BI connector and Microsoft Graph automation.

units.title: Monitor app deployment and troubleshoot failures
points: The app overview shows Installed, Not installed, Failed, Install pending and Not applicable for devices and users.
Failures on all targets suggest packaging, command line, assignment or requirements; failures on some devices suggest device state, edition, architecture or prerequisites.
App installs but Intune reports failure → detection rule mismatch.
Use **Collect diagnostics** for failed Win32 installs and review IME logs (IntuneManagementExtension.log, AppWorkload.log, AppActionProcessor.log, AgentExecutor.log).

units.title: Manage app deployment failures using logs and troubleshooting tools
points: Troubleshoot + support: search user, select device, open failed applications to reach the User install status view; sync the device to retry a Required app.
AppWorkload.log is the key file for install failures and records installer exit codes; read logs with CMTrace or OneTrace (Support Center Log Viewer).
Exclude the IME Content folder and `C:\windows\IMECache` from antimalware scanning to avoid unpredictable failures.
Common codes: `0x87D1041C` app no longer detected (likely uninstalled by user), `0x80073CFF` sideloading not enabled.
The IME installs automatically when the first Win32 app or PowerShell script is assigned; a missing IME can leave apps pending.

keyTerms.definition: Package format created by the Win32 Content Prep Tool from a Win32 installer and its files.
File, registry or MSI product code check that tells Intune whether a Win32 app is installed.
Relationship where a newer app version replaces (uninstalls) an older one; max 10 nodes in a chain.
Rule that includes or excludes devices in an assigned group by properties such as OS version, ownership or model.
Windows agent that installs Win32, Store (new) and WinGet apps and runs scripts; writes logs under ProgramData.
Release cadence for Microsoft 365 Apps: Current, Monthly Enterprise or Semi-Annual Enterprise.

tables.title: Windows app types in Intune
rows: High: detection rules, return codes, dependencies
MSI, APPX/MSIX (other platforms: IPA, APK, PKG)

remember: Need to control or delay updates → **Win32/LOB**, not Microsoft Store apps.
Removing a user from the group ≠ uninstall → use an **Uninstall** assignment.
App installed but status says Failed → check the **detection rule**, not the installer.
Paid Store apps → Enterprise App Catalog, Win32 or volume licensing; **Store for Business is retired**.

selfCheck.q: A Win32 installer returns 3010 and Intune keeps retrying. What do you change?
selfCheck.a: Configure 3010 as a restart-required return code in the app's return codes so Intune treats the install as completed pending restart.

selfCheck.q: A shared lab PC needs a Store app available to every user who signs in. Which install context?
selfCheck.a: System context, which installs or provisions the app at device level.

selfCheck.q: A user reports a Required Win32 app failed. Where do you look on the device for the installer exit code?
selfCheck.a: AppWorkload.log in C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\IntuneManagementExtension\Logs.

modules.title: Implement application protection and security using Microsoft Intune
modules.learnSummary: Plan, configure, assign, monitor, and troubleshoot Microsoft Intune Mobile Application Management (MAM) and App Protection Policies to secure corporate data on BYOD and corporate devices.
modules.tldr: App protection policies (APP) secure corporate data inside MAM-enlightened apps such as Outlook, Teams and Edge, on both unenrolled BYOD devices (MAM-WE) and enrolled corporate devices. They combine data protection, access requirements and conditional launch, are assigned to user groups, and need Microsoft Entra Conditional Access (**Require app protection policy**) to stop users bypassing them with native apps.
objectives: Distinguish Mobile Application Management (MAM) from Mobile Device Management (MDM) and identify when to use App Protection Policies
Plan and configure App Protection Policies for unenrolled BYOD and enrolled corporate devices
Define data protection, encryption, app restriction, access requirement, and conditional launch settings
Use Microsoft Entra Conditional Access to enforce App Protection at sign-in
Assign, monitor, and troubleshoot App Protection Policies across your organization
keyPoints: **MDM** secures the device; **MAM/APP** secures the data inside apps. Use APP on BYOD *and* as defense in depth on managed corporate devices.
Apps must be **MAM-enlightened** via the **Intune App SDK** (built into Microsoft 365 mobile apps) or the **App Wrapping Tool** (internal LOB apps).
**MAM-WE**: the policy applies only when the user signs in with their **corporate Entra ID account**; a personal account in the same app is ignored.
Target device state with **Target to apps on all device types = No** and Device types **Unmanaged** (BYOD) or **Managed** (enrolled).
Typical data protection: send org data to **Policy managed apps**, block Save copies (allow OneDrive for Business/SharePoint), cut/copy/paste **Policy managed apps with paste in**.
Conditional launch actions: **Warn**, **Block access** (no data deleted) or **Wipe data** (a selective wipe of corporate data only).
APPs are assigned to **user groups**; when two policies conflict, the **most restrictive** setting wins.
Enforce with Conditional Access grant **Require app protection policy** — the older *Require approved client app* was retired.

units.title: Understand Mobile Application Management (MAM) and App Protection Policies
points: MAM manages apps and their data without touching personal photos, texts or browsing history.
MAM-enlightened apps become managed apps isolated from unmanaged apps by a cryptographic boundary.
APP layers: data relocation, access requirements (PIN/biometrics), conditional launch (jailbreak, OS version, offline time).
Selective wipe removes only corporate data from managed apps when an employee leaves.

units.title: Plan application protection strategies for BYOD and corporate devices
points: BYOD: MAM-WE with no enrollment, block copy/paste to personal apps, require an app PIN.
Corporate: MDM plus an APP targeting managed devices prevents leaks to user-installed personal apps.
Three-tier framework: Level 1 Enterprise basic, Level 2 Enterprise enhanced, Level 3 Enterprise high (adds stricter PIN, blocks third-party keyboards and printing, MTD integration).
BYOD typically Level 2; corporate Level 1 or 2; high-security roles (finance, healthcare, executives) Level 3.
Windows MAM has no app PIN and no jailbreak detection; access is controlled by Entra ID sign-in.

units.title: Configure App Protection Policies for unenrolled BYOD devices
points: Supported on iOS/iPadOS, Android and Windows 10/11; Windows MAM covers Microsoft Edge for Business and Microsoft 365 Apps and relies on OAuth2 token protection.
Create in **Apps > App protection policies**; set Device types to **Unmanaged**.
Require PIN, allow biometrics, block jailbroken/rooted devices, offline grace: block after 12 hours, wipe after 90 days.
Offboarding: **Apps > App selective wipe > Create wipe request** for the user and device.

units.title: Configure App Protection Policies for enrolled corporate devices
points: Set Device types to **Managed** so the policy applies only to MDM-enrolled devices.
Relaxed access (app PIN and work credentials not required, because MDM already enforces a device passcode), strict data protection.
If a PIN is used: max 5 attempts, then reset with Entra ID credentials.
Create a separate policy per platform (iOS/iPadOS, Android, Windows); the Windows settings surface differs from mobile.
Policies are assigned to users; Intune evaluates managed vs. unmanaged state at sign-in.

units.title: Define data protection, encryption, and app restriction settings
points: Block syncing policy-managed app data with native apps (keeps corporate contacts out of personal address books).
Device encryption via MDM: BitLocker (keys escrowed to Entra ID), FileVault (key escrowed to Intune), passcode-triggered encryption on iOS/Android.
App-level: **Encrypt org data = Require** for BYOD where full-disk encryption can't be enforced.
Restrict web content transfer to **Microsoft Edge**; block third-party keyboards; block screen capture on Android (iOS can't block screenshots via APP).

units.title: Define access requirements and conditional launch behaviors
points: Access requirements: app PIN separate from the device lock screen, biometrics with PIN fallback, work credentials not required for daily use.
Conditional launch is checked on every launch or resume; each condition has an action (Warn, Block access, Wipe data).
Max allowed threat level (Secured, Low, Medium, High) uses Microsoft Defender or another MTD connector configured under **Tenant administration > Connectors and tokens**.
Disabled Entra ID account → Wipe data; offline 720 minutes → block, 90 days → wipe.

units.title: Configure Conditional Access policies for application access control
points: BYOD policy: Office 365, platforms iOS and Android, client apps *Mobile apps and desktop clients*, grant **Require app protection policy**.
Corporate policy: Windows and macOS, optional device filter `device.deviceOwnership -eq "Company"`, grant **Require device to be marked as compliant**.
Multiple controls: **Require one** (OR) supports both BYOD and corporate; **Require all** (AND) is the strictest.
Exclude break-glass accounts and start in **Report-only**, checking the sign-in logs before turning it on.

units.title: Assign and monitor App Protection Policies
points: Assign to user groups, pilot first, exclude break-glass and service accounts.
Monitor in **Apps > Monitor > App protection status**: Assigned users, Flagged users (PIN lockouts, jailbreak detections), User status.
Check: corporate sign-in, app included in the policy, device-state filter matches, force a sync from the app.

units.title: Troubleshoot application protection policy issues
points: Baseline: user licensed for Intune, targeted via a user group, app is MAM-enlightened (never native Mail apps), corporate identity signed in.
In **Troubleshooting + support > Troubleshoot**, check App protection status, policy name and whether the device is seen as Managed or Unmanaged.
On the device: `about:intunehelp` in Edge shows cached policies and sends MAM logs; Outlook **Help & Feedback > Collect Diagnostics** gives an incident ID.
Common errors: conflicting policies (most restrictive wins), missing Conditional Access, an app missing from the policy's public apps list.

keyTerms.definition: MAM without enrollment: app protection on devices not enrolled in Intune, triggered by corporate sign-in.
An app that supports Intune policies through the Intune App SDK or App Wrapping Tool.
Removes only corporate data and keys from managed apps, leaving personal data intact.
APP health checks on each app launch (jailbreak, OS/app version, threat level, offline time) with Warn, Block or Wipe actions.

keyTerms.term: Policy managed apps with paste in
keyTerms.definition: Clipboard setting that allows pasting into managed apps but blocks copying corporate data out.
Conditional Access grant control that only allows access from apps with an Intune APP applied; replaces Require approved client app.

tables.title: APP baseline by device type
rows: Send org data to other apps
Allow OneDrive for Business / SharePoint only
Policy managed apps with paste in

tables.title: Conditional launch actions
rows: App opens but data is blocked until remediated

remember: APP assigned to a **device group** → it won't apply; APPs target **users**.
Users still use native iOS Mail → missing **Conditional Access** with *Require app protection policy*.
Policy targets Unmanaged but device is enrolled → policy doesn't apply; build both Managed and Unmanaged policies.
BYOD + corporate in one CA policy → app protection **OR** compliant device (*Require one of the selected controls*).

selfCheck.q: An employee with a personal iPhone leaves the company. How do you remove corporate email without touching personal photos?
selfCheck.a: Issue a selective wipe via Apps > App selective wipe for that user and device; only corporate data in managed apps is deleted.

selfCheck.q: A user is in two groups: one APP requires a PIN, the other disables it. What happens?
selfCheck.a: The most restrictive setting applies, so the PIN is required.

selfCheck.q: You want APP to block access when Microsoft Defender detects a high threat on the phone. What must be set up first?
selfCheck.a: The Microsoft Defender (MTD) connector under Tenant administration > Connectors and tokens; then set Max allowed threat level in conditional launch.

modules.title: Manage application lifecycle and user experience using Microsoft Intune
modules.learnSummary: Learn how to manage applications across the full Microsoft Intune lifecycle, including deployment, configuration, protection, monitoring, update, and retirement.
modules.tldr: Intune manages apps through five lifecycle stages: add, deploy, configure, protect and retire. Update behavior differs by app type and platform (Store auto-updates, Win32 supersedence, LOB version checks, Enterprise App Catalog updates, VPP and Managed Google Play update modes). Groups, assignment filters, app configuration policies, app protection plus Conditional Access, and monitoring reports cover the rest of the lifecycle.
objectives: Describe the five stages of the Intune application lifecycle.
Update and retire applications across Windows, iOS/iPadOS, and Android.
Assign applications using groups, filters, and targeting.
Manage user and device groups for application delivery.
Configure default application settings and user experience with app configuration policies.
Enforce compliance requirements using app protection policies and Conditional Access.
Monitor app deployment, usage, and reliability with Intune reports and Endpoint analytics.
keyPoints: The lifecycle is a loop: **Add → Deploy → Configure → Protect → Retire**. Retirement matters as much as deployment.
**LOB updates** are package-based: Intune compares versions and **rejects a package with the same version**.

**Enterprise App Catalog** updates aren't automatic: review *Enterprise App Catalog apps with updates*, create the new app and use **supersedence**. Requires Enterprise Application Management (standalone or Intune Suite).
Managed Google Play update modes: **Default**, **High Priority** (install as soon as possible), **Postponed** (fixed 90 days).
On unenrolled devices you can assign to users only, as Available; **Required, Uninstall, device assignment and Intune app updates need enrollment**.
**Assignment filters** (Tenant administration > Assignment filters) include or exclude devices or apps within a group; managed-app filters apply to app protection and app configuration policies.
**App configuration policies** pre-set app settings via the **Managed devices** (MDM channel, iOS/Android) or **Managed apps** (MAM channel, no enrollment; on Windows only Edge) channel.
**Discovered apps** is the software inventory: personal devices report managed apps only; refresh every 7 days, or 24 hours for Win32 via the IME.

units.title: Understand application lifecycle management in Microsoft Intune
points: Intune manages apps on Android, iOS/iPadOS, macOS and Windows, including store, LOB, built-in and web apps.
Add makes the app a managed object; Deploy assigns it to users or devices.
Configure pre-defines settings (e.g. app configuration policies, Edge settings); Protect uses Conditional Access and app protection policies, also on unenrolled devices.
Retire uninstalls and removes apps that are outdated or replaced.

units.title: Update and retire applications in Microsoft Intune
points: Microsoft Store app (new) updates automatically; for Available apps, Intune manages updates once the user installs from Company Portal.
Apple VPP: **Prevent automatic app updates** on the assignment works only when the token's Automatic app updates is on; switching Required to Available stops auto-updates of installed copies.
Android unmanaged devices: removing the work account leaves Play Store apps installed.
iOS/iPadOS **Uninstall on device removal** controls managed apps on unenrollment.
App selective wipe removes work data from protected apps; the **Retire** device action removes company data, profiles and many apps (IME-installed Win32 apps aren't uninstalled on Windows).

units.title: Assign applications using groups, filters, and targeting
points: Intents: Required, Available for enrolled devices, Available with or without enrollment (needs an Intune licence), Uninstall.
Uninstall only removes apps Intune installed through the same deployment.
Group mode lets you include or exclude groups.
Filter example: osVersion equals 10.0.26200 AND manufacturer equals Microsoft; then set filter mode to Include or Exclude filtered devices.
Filters work for managed devices on Android (device administrator, Enterprise, AOSP), iOS/iPadOS, macOS and Windows, and for managed apps on Android, iOS/iPadOS and Windows.

units.title: Manage user and device groups for application delivery
points: User groups give consistent app access across a user's devices; device groups fit shared devices and specific hardware.
Available is intended for user groups on most platforms; Win32 apps can be Available to user or device groups; Android Enterprise COBO/COPE also support device groups.
When intents conflict across groups, required is prioritized over available.
Best practices: nested and dynamic groups, regular membership reviews, test small first, monitor install status.

units.title: Configure default application settings and user experience
points: App configuration policies push settings before users run the app: security, branding, language, connectivity, features.
Managed devices channel: enrolled iOS/iPadOS and Android, e.g. account setup, work-or-school-only accounts, S/MIME.
Managed apps channel: SDK/wrapped apps on iOS/iPadOS, Android and Windows (Edge only), no enrollment needed; typically user-assigned.
Example: **Apps > Configuration > Create > Managed devices**, Android Enterprise Outlook with modern authentication and work-or-school accounts only.
Check vendor docs for supported settings, pilot first, avoid setting the same value in multiple ways.

units.title: Enforce compliance requirements for applications
points: Combine app protection policies, Conditional Access and (if needed) device compliance policies.
App-based Conditional Access requires an APP before users can access selected cloud resources.

Example Outlook Android policy: block Android backup, encrypt org data, PIN with biometrics, max 5 PIN attempts → Reset PIN, block access offline after 1440 minutes, wipe after 90 days, block rooted devices, Samsung Knox attestation.
Create separate APPs for enrolled and unenrolled devices and use managed-app filters to target each.

units.title: Monitor app lifecycle and usage analytics
points: App overview shows Installed, Not Installed, Failed, Install Pending, Not Applicable; Store and Android Store apps deployed as Available don't report install status.
**Apps > Monitor > Discovered apps**: name, platform, version, device count, publisher; exportable to CSV.
**Apps > Monitor > App protection status** shows policy, compliance state and last sync; data kept at least 90 days.
**Reports > Endpoint analytics > Application reliability**: App performance tab covers the last 14 days of usage and failures.

keyTerms.definition: A newer Win32 app updates or replaces an older Win32 app.
Microsoft-hosted, prepared Win32 apps with prefilled install, detection and requirement settings; part of Enterprise Application Management.
Reusable rule on device or app properties used in Include or Exclude mode on an assignment.
Policy that pre-sets app settings through the managed devices (MDM) or managed apps (MAM) channel.
Software inventory report of apps detected on enrolled devices.
Removes company data, managed settings, profiles and many Intune apps while keeping personal data.

tables.title: Assignment options: enrolled vs. not enrolled
App configuration channels
rows: Account setup, work-or-school-only accounts, S/MIME, general settings
General settings, S/MIME, advanced data protection extending APP

remember: Uploaded a LOB package and Intune refuses it → the **version number** is the same as the stored one.
Need to test a new Android app version first → Managed Google Play **Postponed** (90 days, not configurable).
Enterprise App Catalog has a newer version → it's **not** applied automatically; create the new app and supersede.
Unenrolled device → no Required, no Uninstall, no device assignment.

selfCheck.q: A critical security fix for a Managed Google Play app must install immediately on fully managed Android devices. Which update mode?
selfCheck.a: High Priority, which installs the update as soon as possible after release, bypassing the default conditions.

selfCheck.q: You want Outlook on enrolled Android Enterprise devices to configure email automatically and allow only work accounts. What do you create?
selfCheck.a: An app configuration policy for Managed devices (Apps > Configuration), using modern authentication and allowing only work or school accounts.

selfCheck.q: Where do you find which desktop apps crash most often over the last 14 days?
selfCheck.a: Endpoint analytics Application reliability report, App performance tab (Reports > Endpoint analytics > Application reliability).

modules.title: Monitor and optimize application performance using Microsoft Intune
modules.learnSummary: Monitor application health, deployment status, and performance across managed devices using Microsoft Intune reports and Endpoint analytics.
modules.tldr: App health means install success, crash frequency (reliability) and startup impact, measured continuously in production instead of only tested before deployment. Intune app reports (app overview, Device/User install status, App Install Status) show deployment status and error codes, while Endpoint analytics measures reliability and startup performance against baselines. You turn the data into prioritized, playbook-driven fixes and then verify the improvement in the same reports.
objectives: Describe app health and performance metrics in modern endpoint environments.
Monitor app deployment status and compliance using Intune reports.
Track installation success and failure rates with detailed error reporting.
Use Endpoint analytics to measure app performance, startup impact, and reliability trends.
Use Intune reporting tools to identify and resolve performance issues.
Optimize the user experience by applying actionable insights from monitoring data.
keyPoints: App health has three dimensions: **installation success**, **reliability** (crash frequency, mean time between failures) and **startup impact**.
Use **baselines** to separate normal variation from real problems and avoid alert fatigue.
The app overview shows **Installed, Not Installed, Failed, Install Pending, Not Applicable** for devices and users; check **last check-in** before trusting a status.
Store and Android Store apps deployed as **Available don't report install status** unless the user installs them.
Look at **failure rates and trends**, not raw counts: 10 of 500 is 2%, 25 of 50 is 50%.

**Endpoint analytics** (Reports > Endpoint analytics) needs Windows 10/11 Pro, Education or Enterprise, Intune enrollment or co-management, and the **Connected User Experiences and Telemetry** service running.
Intune has **no built-in alerting** for app failures; export data (e.g. Microsoft Graph export jobs) to Azure Monitor/Log Analytics to alert.
Prioritize by **severity, scope, remediation difficulty and business criticality**, then validate fixes after one or two check-in cycles.

units.title: Understand app health and performance in modern environments
points: Remote work, personal devices and varied networks make production performance hard to predict.
Intune collects install status, crash reports, performance measurements and user impact from enrolled devices.
Startup impact scores show how much an app delays boot; 5 extra seconds × 1,000 daily restarts adds up to hours a week.
Modern monitoring validates performance continuously in production instead of once before deployment.

units.title: Monitor app deployment and compliance using Intune
points: **Apps > All Apps > [app]**: Essentials (publisher, OS, version, MAM SDK use, assignment) plus device and user status graphs.
Device install status: device, user, platform, app version, status details and last check-in. User install status aggregates a user's devices.
Required apps are tracked for compliance; with Conditional Access you can block access until required apps are installed.
LOB, Win32 and Required apps always report detailed status; Managed Google Play apps in work profiles also report the version.
The Apps overview tiles show tenant-wide installation failures to spot sudden spikes.

units.title: Track installation success and failure reports
points: **Apps > Monitor > App Install Status** lists every app with install and failure counts; sort by failures to prioritize.
AOSP and Android Enterprise fully managed/dedicated LOB failures give detailed codes showing retry and whether the user can act (e.g. `0x87D54FB7` low storage, `0x87D54FB4` corrupt APK).
Download failures (network, temporary storage) differ from installation failures.
User-actionable errors → education/self-service; IT-actionable → fix the package or dependencies; environmental → firewall, proxy, bandwidth.

units.title: Use Endpoint Analytics to measure app performance and startup times
points: **Application Reliability** ranks apps by crashes, affected devices and mean time between failures; **Startup Performance** shows boot times and per-app startup impact.
The Overview score is color-coded (green, yellow, red) for a quick health view.
Reliability and Startup Performance are in standard Intune licensing; Advanced Analytics (Intune Suite or standalone add-on) adds Device query, Enhanced device timeline and Anomaly detection.
Read access: Help Desk Operator, Read Only Operator, Endpoint Security Manager, School Administrator, and the Entra **Reports Reader** role.
Act on insights: disable unnecessary startup apps, patch crashing apps, contact vendors.

units.title: Use Intune reporting tools to identify and resolve performance issues
points: Four report categories: Operational, Organizational, Historical, Specialist.
App Install Status is operational; the per-device **Managed Apps** report shows installed apps, versions and history.
Reports reflect the last check-in; use **Generate Report** to refresh where available.

**Reports > Diagnostic settings** sends Intune diagnostic logs to Log Analytics (KQL), but these **don't include app install status** — export that separately. Costs depend on data volume and retention.

units.title: Optimize user experience with actionable insights
points: Translate metrics into business impact so stakeholders understand them.
Prioritize by severity, scope, remediation difficulty and business criticality; don't ignore small-scope issues for critical roles.
Write remediation playbooks for user-actionable, compatibility and infrastructure problems.
Proactive measures: pilot groups, update test rings, storage capacity management.
Measure before/after and hold weekly operational, monthly tactical and quarterly strategic reviews.

keyTerms.definition: Intune service that measures startup performance, app reliability and user experience on Windows devices.
How many seconds an application adds to the device boot process.
Organizational average used to judge whether a metric is normal or problematic.
Tenant-wide report of install and failure counts for every app (Apps > Monitor).
Intune setting that streams supported log categories to a Log Analytics workspace.

tables.title: Intune report categories
rows: Timely, targeted data for immediate action
Devices with app failures right now
Broader summaries for managers and planners
Deciding whether to upgrade aging devices

remember: Available Store app shows no status → **by design**, not a failure.
Device missing from Endpoint analytics → check the **Connected User Experiences and Telemetry** service and the Windows edition.
Alerts on app failures → **export + Azure Monitor**; Intune diagnostic settings alone don't contain install status.
Install Pending for days with no check-in → status is probably **stale**, not active.

selfCheck.q: Users complain that devices take long to boot after a new app rollout. Which report shows which app is responsible?
selfCheck.a: The Endpoint analytics Startup Performance report, which shows per-app startup impact.

selfCheck.q: A help desk operator needs to view Endpoint analytics data without admin rights. What can you assign?
selfCheck.a: An Intune role such as Help Desk Operator or Read Only Operator, or the Microsoft Entra Reports Reader role.

selfCheck.q: An Android LOB app on a dedicated device fails with code 0x87D54FB7. Who can fix it?
selfCheck.a: The user: it means insufficient storage, so freeing space resolves it, and Intune retries.

modules.title: Manage Enterprise App Catalog applications
modules.learnSummary: Discover, deploy, configure, update, and monitor prepackaged Win32 applications from the Microsoft Intune Enterprise App Catalog.
modules.tldr: The Enterprise App Catalog provides prepackaged Win32 apps with install/uninstall commands, restart behavior, requirements and detection rules already filled in, so you don't have to package them yourself. Catalog apps aren't updated automatically: you review available updates and use guided supersedence to move devices to the new version (self-updating apps are only validated). The device-level Managed Apps report confirms the version, resolved intent and install status.
objectives: Discover and deploy applications from the Enterprise App Catalog
Configure default install commands, detection rules, and requirements for catalog apps
Monitor catalog app updates and use supersedence to transition devices to newer versions
Use the Managed Apps report to verify deployment status and troubleshoot catalog app issues
keyPoints: The catalog is part of **Microsoft Intune Enterprise Application Management** — a standalone add-on or included in **Intune Suite**.
Add via **Apps > All apps > Create > Other > Enterprise App Catalog app**, then search the catalog and pick a configuration package.
Intune **prepopulates** install/uninstall commands, restart behavior, detection rules and requirements (OS version, architecture).
Review the defaults and **keep overrides minimal**; restart behavior is usually **No specific action** or **Suppress**. Pilot any change.
Catalog apps are **not updated automatically**: use **Apps > Enterprise App Catalog apps with updates > Update > Supersede app**.
**Self-updating** apps update through the vendor's mechanism; Intune only checks the detected version meets the minimum.
Update availability target: most updates within **24 hours** of vendor release, manually validated ones within **7 days**.
**Managed Apps** report (Devices > All devices > [device] > Managed Apps) shows app name, version, **resolved intent** and install status.

units.title: Discover and deploy apps from the catalog
points: Catalog apps are prepackaged Win32 apps for managed Windows devices.
Search the catalog (e.g. 7-Zip), review publisher, version and description, then select a configuration package.
Wizard: App information → Program → Requirements → Detection rules → Supersedence (optionally uninstall previous version) → Assignments.

units.title: Configure default install and detection settings
points: Program pane: check silent install command, uninstall command, restart behavior and system vs. user context.
Detection rules use a file, registry setting or MSI product code; multiple rules must refer to the same product.
Reliable detection decides install status, remediation and deployment health.
Adjust only for custom install folders, a different target version, nonstandard architecture or a required restart.

units.title: Monitor updates and supersedence
points: Supersedence lets a newer Win32 app update or replace an older version or a different Win32 app.
See updates under **Apps > Enterprise App Catalog apps with updates** or the app's Overview tile.
**Supersede app** creates a new app with the latest package and sets the supersedence relationship; then assign and create.
Monitor the rollout with the device Managed Apps report.

units.title: Use the Managed Apps report for insights
points: Device-level view of apps installed, not installed or available for install.
Use it when users say an app is missing, not updated or not working.
Supports updates (are devices on the new version?) and retirement (is the old app still present?).
Compare version and status of the same catalog app on a few test devices after deployment.

keyTerms.definition: Microsoft-provided set of prepackaged Win32 apps with prefilled deployment settings.
Intune add-on (standalone or in Intune Suite) that includes the Enterprise App Catalog.
Update workflow that creates a new catalog app with the latest package and links it to the old app.
Catalog app updated by the vendor's own mechanism; Intune validates the minimum version.
The effective assignment intent for an app on a device, shown in the Managed Apps report.

remember: New version in the catalog ≠ new version on devices → you must **supersede**.
Catalog apps are **Win32** apps → same detection, requirements and IME logic as other Win32 apps.
Check one device's catalog app version → **Managed Apps** report on the device, not the tenant-wide summary.

selfCheck.q: A new 7-Zip version appears in the catalog. How do you get it to devices?
selfCheck.a: Go to Apps > Enterprise App Catalog apps with updates, select the app, choose Update > Supersede app, assign it and create.

selfCheck.q: Which licence is needed to use the Enterprise App Catalog?
selfCheck.a: Microsoft Intune Enterprise Application Management, as a standalone add-on or through Microsoft Intune Suite.

selfCheck.q: A user says a catalog app is still on the old version. Where do you check first?
selfCheck.a: The device's Managed Apps report, which shows the installed version, resolved intent and install status.

modules.title: Implement endpoint security with Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Intune
modules.learnSummary: Onboard devices to Microsoft Defender with Microsoft Intune, configure security baselines and EDR policies, and investigate and triage incidents in the Microsoft Defender portal.
modules.tldr: Microsoft Defender provides the threat detection, investigation and response for endpoints; Intune onboards devices and deploys the security policies. You connect the two services once, onboard devices with an EDR policy, then configure baselines, antivirus, firewall and ASR separately. Incidents are investigated, triaged and escalated in the Microsoft Defender portal.
objectives: Describe how Microsoft Defender protects endpoints, including its architecture, components, and security capabilities
Onboard Windows, macOS, and mobile devices to Microsoft Defender using Microsoft Intune
Configure security baselines, antivirus, firewall, and attack surface reduction policies
Deploy and manage Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) policies across supported platforms
Investigate and respond to endpoint threats from the Microsoft Defender portal
Monitor and triage security incidents in the Microsoft Defender portal
keyPoints: Defender architecture: **endpoint sensors** collect telemetry, the **cloud service** analyzes it, and **integration points** (Defender portal, Intune) correlate signals and enforce policy.
**Intune manages and deploys**, **Defender detects and responds**; Defender's device risk signal can mark a device **noncompliant**, and Conditional Access then blocks access.
The **Intune–Defender service connection** is a one-time tenant setting: turn on **Microsoft Intune connection** under Advanced features in the Defender portal.
Windows onboarding uses an Intune **Endpoint detection and response policy**, ideally with **Auto from connector** to fetch the onboarding package automatically.
**Onboarding is not full protection**: antivirus, ASR rules, firewall and web protection must be deployed separately through endpoint security policies.
Roll out **ASR rules in audit mode** first, review results, add exclusions only if needed, then switch to block mode.
**EDR in block mode** (Defender portal, requires Plan 2) remediates threats when a non-Microsoft antivirus is primary and Defender Antivirus runs passive.
Defender correlates **alerts into incidents**; analysts triage, assign, tag, classify and escalate from the **incident queue**.

units.title: Understand how Microsoft Defender protects endpoints
points: Cross-platform protection (Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS) with central visibility in the Microsoft Defender portal.
Three components: endpoint sensors (local telemetry), cloud service (threat intelligence, behavioral analytics, AI) and integration points with other Microsoft security solutions.
Capabilities: next-generation protection, EDR, attack surface reduction, vulnerability management, automated investigation and remediation, advanced hunting.
Risk-based strategy: Defender sends device risk to Intune, compliance marks risky devices noncompliant and Conditional Access blocks or limits access until remediated.

units.title: Onboard devices to Microsoft Defender using Intune
points: Prerequisites: Intune and Defender for Endpoint licences, devices enrolled and Entra joined or hybrid joined, service connection, and the right permissions.
Connect: Defender portal > System > Settings > Endpoints > General > Advanced features > Microsoft Intune connection.
Windows: Endpoint security > Endpoint detection and response; use the preconfigured policy on the **EDR Onboarding Status** tab or a custom EDR policy.
macOS: deploy the Defender app plus the onboarding package (downloaded from the Defender portal) and profiles for system extensions, network filtering, Full Disk Access, etc.
Android and iOS/iPadOS: onboarded as mobile threat defense by deploying the Defender app and app/device configuration; avoid overlapping onboarding policies.

units.title: Configure Microsoft Defender endpoint security settings and baselines
points: Endpoint security > Security baselines > Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Security Baseline; pilot it with a small group and watch for conflicts with other policies.
Antivirus policy: real-time and cloud-delivered protection, sample submission, scans and exclusions (keep exclusions narrow).
Tamper Protection stops users, scripts or malware from changing protected Defender settings.
ASR profiles need Windows with Defender Antivirus as primary antivirus; firewall policies cover Windows and macOS.

units.title: Configure Endpoint Detection and Response policies
points: Windows EDR settings: client configuration package type (onboard/offboard, **Auto from connector**), manual onboarding package, sample sharing; telemetry reporting frequency is deprecated.
macOS and Linux EDR policies support device tags; Linux also has a Global Exclusions (AV+EDR) profile.
Use the preconfigured policy for quick standard onboarding, a custom policy for control over assignments, scope tags and sample sharing.
EDR in block mode is enabled in the Defender portal (Advanced features) and requires Defender for Endpoint Plan 2.

units.title: Investigate and respond to endpoint threats using Microsoft Defender
points: Alerts are single detections; Defender correlates related alerts into incidents with entities, timeline, evidence and remediation status.
Investigate processes, command lines, files, registry changes, network connections and the device page timeline; the attack story and incident graph show relationships.
Device response actions: automated investigation, Live Response, investigation package, antivirus scan, restrict app execution, isolate or contain device.
AIR assigns verdicts and remediates automatically or after approval in the **Action center**; Security Copilot and promptbooks assist but Defender remains the primary tool.

units.title: Monitor and triage incidents in the Microsoft Defender portal
points: Incident queue: Investigation & response > Incidents & alerts > Incidents; filter and sort by severity, status, owner, assets and detection source.
Triage answers: what happened, which assets, is it active, what's the business impact, what next.
Manage incidents by assigning an owner, tagging, commenting, updating status and classifying.
Escalate (privileged accounts, critical servers, data theft) with enough context so the next responder doesn't repeat the work.

keyTerms.definition: Endpoint detection and response — detailed endpoint telemetry and tools to detect and investigate advanced threats.
EDR policy option that pulls the current onboarding package through the Intune–Defender service connection.
Rules that block common attack behaviors such as malicious scripts or executable content launched from Office apps.
Prevents unauthorized changes to protected Defender security settings.
Lets EDR remediate malicious artifacts when Defender Antivirus runs in passive mode behind another antivirus.
Automated investigation and response — analyzes evidence, assigns verdicts and recommends or takes remediation actions.
A group of correlated alerts that tells the broader attack story.

tables.title: Onboarding to Defender by platform
rows: Endpoint detection and response policy (preconfigured or custom), Auto from connector
Defender app + onboarding package from the Defender portal as configuration profile, plus permission profiles
Defender app deployed through Intune with app/device configuration (mobile threat defense)

remember: Onboarded ≠ protected → onboarding only enables **telemetry**; AV, ASR and firewall come from separate endpoint security policies.
Third-party AV is primary and Defender is passive → think **EDR in block mode** (Plan 2), configured in the Defender portal, not Intune.
ASR rules require **Defender Antivirus as the primary AV** on Windows; start in **audit** before block.
Pending remediation actions waiting for approval → look in the **Action center**.

selfCheck.q: You want Intune to retrieve the Defender onboarding package automatically for Windows devices. What do you need?
selfCheck.a: An active Intune–Defender service connection and an EDR policy using **Auto from connector**.

selfCheck.q: A device is confirmed compromised and the threat is spreading. Which response action limits it fastest?
selfCheck.a: Isolate (or contain) the device from its device page in the Microsoft Defender portal.

selfCheck.q: Devices were onboarded with an EDR policy but ASR rules don't apply. Why?
selfCheck.a: Onboarding doesn't configure ASR; you must deploy an attack surface reduction policy separately (and Defender Antivirus must be primary).

modules.title: Implement device encryption and security policies using Microsoft Intune
modules.learnSummary: Deploy and manage BitLocker device encryption on Windows endpoints using Microsoft Intune, including policy configuration, recovery key management, and compliance monitoring.
modules.tldr: BitLocker protects data at rest so a lost or stolen Windows device doesn't become a data exposure. Configure it in Intune (ideally an Endpoint security disk encryption policy), escrow recovery keys to Microsoft Entra ID, and rotate keys after they're disclosed. Verify the result with the Intune encryption report, compliance status and Defender advanced hunting.
objectives: Explain why device encryption is a regulatory requirement and a security best practice.
Configure BitLocker policies in Intune with appropriate protection levels.
Manage BitLocker recovery keys and enable user self-service recovery.
Monitor encryption compliance across your Windows devices.
Use audit tools in Microsoft Defender to verify endpoint encryption status.
keyPoints: A login password protects only the running OS; **full-disk encryption** (BitLocker, FileVault) keeps a removed drive unreadable. Encryption covers **data at rest**, not in transit or in use.
Zero Trust loop: **compliance policy** checks encryption → device marked **noncompliant** → **Conditional Access** blocks access until re-encrypted.
Prefer **Endpoint security > Disk encryption** for BitLocker; the settings catalog works but makes policy review more complex.
**TPM-only** startup enables silent encryption with no prompts; **TPM + PIN** is stronger but adds user interaction.
**Silent encryption** doesn't require the user to be a local admin, but needs TPM, UEFI, Windows Recovery Environment and Entra join state.
Store recovery keys in **Microsoft Entra ID** and **require backup before encryption starts** so a recoverable key always exists.
**Rotate** the recovery password after any disclosure — manually with the **BitLocker key rotation** remote action or automatically via policy.
**Personal Data Encryption (PDE)** complements BitLocker on Windows 11 22H2+, protecting user folders with Windows Hello credentials; it has no admin recovery key.

units.title: Understand the importance of device encryption for compliance and security
points: Without encryption, an attacker can remove the SSD or boot from USB and read all files and cached credentials.
An encrypted lost laptop dramatically reduces exposure risk, which can affect notification obligations (decided by legal and compliance teams).
Intune compliance evaluates encryption, flags noncompliance and Conditional Access revokes access.
Automated key escrow: the device sends its unique recovery key to its Entra ID device object; helpdesk or users (My Account) retrieve it.

units.title: Configure BitLocker policies using Microsoft Intune
points: Configure OS, fixed data and removable drives; encryption method XTS-AES 128 or 256-bit applies when encryption first starts.
Windows **Automatic Device Encryption (ADE)** can encrypt during OOBE before Intune policy arrives (broader from Windows 11 24H2); a method mismatch shows as encrypted with a profile error.
Changing the encryption method on an already encrypted drive can require decrypting and re-encrypting.
Assign to devices for corporate/shared devices or to users so encryption follows the user; choose silent or standard enablement.
PDE is configured under Disk encryption > Windows > Personal Data Encryption, protecting Desktop, Documents and Pictures; recover lost PDE files from backup.

units.title: Manage BitLocker recovery keys and user self-service options
points: Recommended: save recovery info to Entra ID, require it before BitLocker starts, use a 48-digit recovery password.
Self-service: users select the device in Company Portal and choose **Get recovery key**; tenant settings control Entra self-service.
Least privilege: Helpdesk Administrator or Cloud Device Administrator can read keys, or a custom role with `microsoft.directory/bitlockerKeys/key/read`; every read is audited.
Helpdesk verifies the user, records device name and recovery key ID, and documents the reason.
**Configure Recovery Password Rotation**: off by default, or on for Entra joined, or for Entra joined and hybrid joined devices (Windows 10 1909+).

units.title: Monitor BitLocker compliance and encryption status in Microsoft Intune
points: Devices > Monitor > **Device encryption status** shows TPM version, encryption readiness, encryption status and profile details.
Readiness (can it be encrypted?) differs from status (is the OS drive encrypted?): Ready, Not ready, Not applicable.
Compliance settings: **Require BitLocker** (health attestation, may need a reboot) and **Encryption of data storage on a device**.
Export to CSV to find fleet patterns, e.g. many Not ready devices pointing to TPM or firmware issues.

units.title: Audit device encryption with Microsoft Defender
points: Advanced hunting (KQL) plus Defender Vulnerability Management secure configuration assessments give a security operations view of encryption.
Tables: `DeviceTvmSecureConfigurationAssessment` (per-device `IsApplicable`/`IsCompliant`), `...AssessmentKB` (names, risk, remediation), `DeviceTvmInfoGathering` (inventory).
First discover encryption-related configurations in the KB instead of hard-coding IDs, then query device results.
Flag anomalies: failed controls, stale assessments (e.g. older than 7 days), high-impact failures; correlate with Intune before acting.

keyTerms.definition: Encrypts the whole drive (BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS) so data is unreadable without the key.
Hardware security chip that validates device state at startup before releasing the BitLocker key.
The device backs up its recovery password to a trusted service (Microsoft Entra ID) before or during encryption.
Intune-driven BitLocker enablement without user prompts or local admin rights.
Windows behavior that encrypts the OS drive during OOBE, before Intune policy applies.
Windows 11 file-level protection for selected user folders, unlocked by Windows Hello sign-in.
Whether a device can support policy-driven encryption, separate from whether it is encrypted.

tables.title: BitLocker vs Personal Data Encryption
rows: At startup when protectors (TPM, PIN) are satisfied
After the user signs in with Windows Hello
Powered-on or locked device with sensitive user files
48-digit recovery key escrowed in Entra ID
No admin recovery key — restore from backup

tables.title: Reading the encryption report
rows: Check user action required, recent check-in, encryption in progress
Review TPM, Windows Recovery Environment, OS support, policy
Compare encryption method/protectors with policy (often ADE mismatch)
Sync the device and wait for check-in

remember: Key was read by the helpdesk → **rotate it** (BitLocker key rotation remote action); a disclosed key shouldn't stay valid.
Encrypted device shows a profile error → think **ADE / encryption method mismatch**, not a failed assignment.
Encrypted but still noncompliant → **Require BitLocker** uses health attestation; sync and **reboot**.
PDE **does not replace** BitLocker and has no admin-retrievable recovery key.

selfCheck.q: You want BitLocker to start only when a recovery key is safely stored. Which setting do you configure?
selfCheck.a: Save recovery information to Microsoft Entra ID and require it to be stored before BitLocker is enabled.

selfCheck.q: A helpdesk team must read recovery keys without broader admin rights. What do you assign?
selfCheck.a: A least-privilege role such as Helpdesk Administrator or Cloud Device Administrator, or a custom role with the bitlockerKeys/key/read permission.

selfCheck.q: Users should encrypt without prompts and without being local admins. Which startup authentication fits?
selfCheck.a: TPM-only with silent encryption; TPM + PIN would add user interaction.

modules.title: Implement advanced threat protection using Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Defender
modules.learnSummary: Apply layered endpoint defenses by combining Microsoft Intune policy enforcement with Microsoft Defender for SaaS app discovery, Attack Surface Reduction rules, Zero Trust device access, and proactive remediation.
modules.tldr: Advanced attacks chain several techniques, so endpoint protection layers prevention, detection, response and recovery. Intune enforces policy (baselines, ASR rules, compliance) while Defender supplies detection, cloud app discovery and device risk. Defender risk feeds Intune compliance, and Conditional Access blocks risky devices — Zero Trust in practice.
objectives: Describe layered threat protection strategies that align Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Defender capabilities
Discover and monitor cloud app usage with Microsoft Defender's SaaS app security
Configure Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules in Microsoft Intune to block risky behaviors
Apply Zero Trust principles by integrating device risk and compliance with Conditional Access
keyPoints: Four layers: **prevention** (baselines, AV, firewall, ASR), **detection**, **response** (isolate, scan, AIR, attack disruption) and **recovery and improvement**.
**Intune** = management and policy layer; **Defender** = detection, security intelligence and response layer.
**Cloud Discovery** finds shadow IT from traffic logs or Defender endpoint signals and scores apps against the **Cloud App Catalog**.
Discovery data: **snapshot reports** (manual log upload), **continuous reports** (log collector), or **Defender endpoint integration** for remote users off the corporate network.
Investigate risky cloud apps **before enforcing** — tag apps **Sanctioned/Unsanctioned** and review OAuth permissions.
ASR rules block misuse of everyday tools (Office child processes, scripts, LSASS credential theft); deploy **pilot → Audit → exclusions → Warn/Block → expand**.
Zero Trust principles: **verify explicitly**, **least privilege access**, **assume breach**.
Enforcement flow: Defender reports **device risk** → Intune marks **noncompliant** → **Conditional Access** blocks until remediated.

units.title: Understand advanced threat protection strategies for endpoint environments
points: Attacks such as ransomware chain phishing, scripts, vulnerable apps and lateral movement, so no single control is enough.
Layers: prevention, detection, response, recovery and improvement — each covers a different attack stage.
Defender correlates endpoint, identity, email and app signals and can contain attacks through automatic attack disruption.
Defender detects active malware → device high risk → Intune compliance → Conditional Access restricts access.

units.title: Discover and monitor cloud apps with Microsoft Defender
points: Review in the Defender portal under **Cloud apps > Cloud discovery**: apps, users, traffic, devices, risk scores, sanction status.
Cloud App Catalog scores apps on compliance, legal, security, privacy and general factors.
Ongoing monitoring: discovery policies (e.g. alert on new risky app), anomaly detection, OAuth app monitoring and app governance.
Responses range from user notification and approving a safer alternative to controlled enforcement.

units.title: Configure Attack Surface Reduction rules using Microsoft Intune
points: Rules target Office child processes, executable content from email, LSASS credential theft, script-launched downloads, vulnerable signed drivers, WMI persistence and impersonated system tools.
Create: Endpoint security > Attack surface reduction > Windows > **Attack Surface Reduction Rules** profile.
Modes: Not configured, Off, Audit (log only), Warn (block with user bypass), Block.
Check deployment status in Intune; review detections in the Defender portal's **Attack Surface Reduction Rules report**.

units.title: Apply Zero Trust principles for endpoint protection
points: A successful sign-in alone isn't enough; device health and compliance must also be verified.
Compliance policies check OS version, encryption, password, jailbreak/root status and Defender device risk level.
Zero Trust is continuous: enroll, apply baselines, enforce compliance, onboard to Defender, monitor risk, remediate, re-evaluate access.
Seven-step cycle ends with remediation before access is restored.

keyTerms.definition: Cloud apps users adopt without IT approval, creating data exposure and compliance risk.
Defender capability that analyzes traffic and endpoint data against the Cloud App Catalog to identify used apps and their risk.
Catalog of apps scored on compliance, legal, security, privacy and general risk factors.
Tags that mark whether a discovered app is approved for use.
Logs what a rule would have blocked without blocking it.
Blocks the behavior but may let the user bypass the block.

tables.title: Cloud Discovery data collection options
rows: Point-in-time view from manually uploaded firewall/proxy/gateway logs
Ongoing visibility via a log collector that uploads logs automatically
Discovery from managed endpoints, including remote users off the corporate network
Data from supported firewalls, proxies and secure web gateways

remember: Remote users not behind the corporate proxy → **Defender endpoint integration** for Cloud Discovery, not snapshot logs.
Test an ASR rule without impacting users → **Audit**; let users override → **Warn**.
Compromised laptop must lose access automatically → Defender **risk level** in an Intune **compliance policy** + Conditional Access requiring a compliant device.

selfCheck.q: You need a one-time view of cloud apps used last month from proxy logs. Which report type?
selfCheck.a: A snapshot report from manually uploaded logs.

selfCheck.q: A line-of-business app might break under a new ASR rule. How do you roll it out?
selfCheck.a: Assign to a pilot group in Audit mode, review events, add exclusions only if needed, then move to Warn or Block.

selfCheck.q: Which Zero Trust principle says to design controls as if an attacker already has access?
selfCheck.a: Assume breach.

modules.title: Enforce compliance and remediate security issues by using Microsoft Intune
modules.learnSummary: Design, assign, and monitor Microsoft Intune compliance policies, configure graduated noncompliance actions, and automate remediation for noncompliant devices.
modules.tldr: Configuration profiles make a device secure; compliance policies prove it is. Intune evaluates static settings and Defender's machine risk score, then Conditional Access enforces the result. Graduated actions for noncompliance, scoping with groups and filters, Remediations and compliance reports turn this into a self-healing, auditable process.
objectives: Explain how compliance policies, configuration profiles, and risk-based evaluation work together to enforce Zero Trust
Create compliance policies for Windows, iOS/iPadOS, Android, and macOS that evaluate device health, OS versions, encryption, and threat levels
Assign and scope compliance policies using Microsoft Entra groups, dynamic groups, and assignment filters
Configure graduated actions for noncompliance, including notifications, grace periods, and automated retirement
Automate remediation using configuration profiles and Intune Remediations to enable self-healing devices
Monitor compliance status and generate reports for operational troubleshooting and audit readiness
keyPoints: **Configuration forces the state; compliance verifies it** — e.g. a BitLocker profile encrypts, a compliance policy checks BitLocker is on.
Intune is the **evaluator**; **Conditional Access** (grant: *Require device to be marked as compliant*) is the **enforcer**. Without it, noncompliant users keep access.
Risk-based compliance: Defender assigns a **machine risk score** (Clear, Low, Medium, High); require the device to be **at or under** a chosen level.
A grace period puts the device **In grace period** — reported honestly, and users **keep access** until it becomes Not compliant.
**Push notifications** work on Android and iOS/iPadOS only (not Windows) and delivery isn't guaranteed; emails use a **notification message template**.
**Assignment filters** narrow a broad group assignment by device properties (e.g. `deviceOwnership -eq "Corporate"`) and avoid group bloat.
**Remediations** (formerly Proactive Remediations) are **Windows-only** detection + remediation PowerShell scripts delivered by the Intune Management Extension.
Set **Mark devices with no compliance policy assigned as** to **Not compliant** — the default Compliant lets unchecked devices through.

units.title: Understand compliance policies and risk-based enforcement
points: Static baseline: device health (Health Attestation, jailbreak/root), min/max OS versions, password, encryption, firewall and antivirus.
Static checks miss active threats, so Intune integrates with Mobile Threat Defense partners and Defender for Endpoint.
When Defender raises the risk to High, Intune marks the device noncompliant without waiting for a scheduled check-in.
End-to-end: phishing → Defender High risk → noncompliant → Conditional Access blocks Teams → user gets remediation instructions.

units.title: Create compliance policies for supported platforms
points: Platform-specific: Windows (Secure Boot, TPM, firewall, AV, risk score), iOS (jailbreak, passcode), Android Enterprise (scope depends on work profile vs fully managed), macOS (FileVault, SIP, Gatekeeper).
Android **Play Integrity** levels: basic, device and strong integrity.
Custom compliance (Windows and macOS) uses a PowerShell or Bash script for checks like a registry key or service; Windows LAPS is configured under Account protection, not compliance.
Create under Devices > Compliance > Policies; use naming conventions like *Win10-Comp-BitLockerRequired* to separate compliance from configuration.

units.title: Assign and scope compliance policies using groups and filters
points: User groups: policy follows the user to every device; device groups: for shared devices and kiosks regardless of who signs in.
Combine included and excluded groups, e.g. All Users minus Executive Team during a phased rollout.
Dynamic groups use attribute rules; they contain users **or** devices, never both, and device rules can't reference user attributes.
Filters (Tenant administration > Filters) run in **Include** or **Exclude** mode and are evaluated at check-in (typically every 8 hours).

units.title: Configure actions for noncompliant devices
points: **Mark device noncompliant** is built in and defaults to 0 days; delay it to create a grace period.
Email action can CC managers, security or helpdesk; templates support logos and variables such as device name.
**Add device to retire list** only lists the device — an admin must initiate retirement; **Retire the noncompliant device** removes corporate data, Wi-Fi profiles and apps.
Example timeline: Day 0 grace period → Day 1 email → Day 3 Not compliant (CA blocks) → Day 7 push → Day 30 retire list.

units.title: Remediate device issues using compliance and configuration policies
points: Declarative configuration profiles reapply drifted settings at the next sync (e.g. a firewall policy turns the firewall back on), so devices self-heal.
Remediations: detection script (exit code 1 = issue) triggers the remediation script; targets Windows Enterprise, Education or Pro, Entra joined or hybrid joined.
macOS uses separate shell scripts (Devices > macOS > Scripts), not Remediations.
Dynamic groups **can't** use compliance status; target with assignment filters (e.g. device category) or assigned groups.
Manual remote actions: Sync, Update Windows Defender Security Intelligence, Restart.

units.title: Monitor and report on compliance results
points: Devices > Compliance > Monitor gives the tenant view; drill into a policy for per-policy results; Reports > Device compliance for exportable data.
Drill from per-device to per-setting to see which rule failed; reports show the last signed-in user, or System account for device-targeted policies.
Filter by compliance state, platform and ownership, then export to .csv or .json; Power BI for advanced dashboards.
Use reports for helpdesk troubleshooting, persistent noncompliance, trends and quarterly audits.

keyTerms.definition: Rules a device must meet to be marked Compliant; it checks state rather than configuring it.
Defender's device risk level (Clear, Low, Medium, High) that Intune compliance can evaluate.
A timed escalation of actions (mark noncompliant, email, push, retire list, retire) for failing devices.
Compliance state during the delay before Not compliant; users keep Conditional Access–protected access.
Device-property rule (Include/Exclude) that narrows a group assignment at check-in.
Windows-only paired detection and remediation PowerShell scripts run by the Intune Management Extension.
Android attestation with basic, device and strong integrity levels.

tables.title: Actions for noncompliance
rows: Built in; default 0 days, delay it for a grace period
Email from a notification message template
Can CC manager, security or helpdesk
Alert via Company Portal or Intune app
Android and iOS/iPadOS only; delivery not guaranteed
Lists device under Retire noncompliant devices
Admin must review and retire manually
Removes corporate data, Wi-Fi profiles and apps

tables.title: Groups vs assignment filters
rows: Policy follows the user to all devices
Applies to personal devices too unless filtered
Kiosks, shared and conference room devices
Users or devices only; can't use compliance status
Narrow a broad assignment by device properties

remember: Device is noncompliant but the user still opens email → no **Conditional Access** policy requiring a compliant device.
Push notification to a Windows laptop → **not supported**; use email.
Custom registry fix on Windows → **Remediations**; on macOS → **shell scripts**.
New device with no compliance policy shows Compliant → change **Mark devices with no compliance policy assigned as** to Not compliant.

selfCheck.q: You want a strict iOS policy to apply only to corporate iPhones, assigned to All Users. How?
selfCheck.a: Add an Include assignment filter with `(device.deviceOwnership -eq "Corporate")`.

selfCheck.q: During a 3-day grace period, can the user still access Conditional Access–protected apps?
selfCheck.a: Yes — the device is In grace period, and access is blocked only once it becomes Not compliant.

selfCheck.q: A user disables the Windows firewall and gets blocked. What restores compliance without a ticket?
selfCheck.a: An endpoint security firewall policy that reapplies the setting at the next sync, after which compliance re-evaluates as healthy.

modules.title: Secure mobile access using Microsoft Tunnel
modules.learnSummary: Learn how to deploy and manage Microsoft Tunnel Gateway to securely extend access to on-premises resources for enrolled and unenrolled mobile devices.
modules.tldr: Microsoft Tunnel Gateway is a containerized VPN service on a Linux server that gives Android and iOS/iPadOS devices access to on-premises resources. You define a server configuration and site in Intune, install the server, deploy the Microsoft Defender app and assign a VPN profile. Tunnel for MAM extends the same gateway to unenrolled BYOD devices through app configuration and app protection policies.
objectives: Deploy Microsoft Tunnel Gateway infrastructure on Linux servers
Configure server settings, sites, and VPN profiles in Intune
Extend Tunnel support to unenrolled mobile devices through Mobile Application Management (MAM)
Monitor Tunnel server health and troubleshoot connectivity issues
keyPoints: Build order: **server configuration → site → install on Linux → deploy Microsoft Defender app → VPN profile**; each step depends on the previous.
A **server configuration** holds network settings (IP range, port 443 TCP/UDP, DNS, split tunneling) and is assigned to a **site**, which groups servers behind one public IP or FQDN.
Use the **APIPA range** `169.254.0.0/16` for client IP leases, and never use `0.0.0.0` in split-tunneling rules.
Install with `mstunnel-setup` as root; the TLS certificate must have the server's IP or FQDN in the **SAN**; sign in with an account that has **Intune Administrator** rights and an Intune licence.
The **Microsoft Defender app** is the tunnel client on Android and iOS/iPadOS; VPN profiles use connection type **Microsoft Tunnel**.
**Tunnel for MAM** serves **unenrolled** devices on the same infrastructure and needs **Intune Plan 2 or the Intune Suite**.
Tunnel for MAM: Android via the Defender app (per-app or device-wide, **no Always-on**); iOS via the **Tunnel for MAM SDK** in LOB apps (**per-app only**).
Operate with **Health status** in the admin center, `mst-cli` on the server and `journalctl` logs.

units.title: Configure Tunnel gateway
points: Server configurations and sites live under Tenant administration > Microsoft Tunnel Gateway; split tunneling allows up to 500 include/exclude rules.
Site settings: public IP/FQDN, server configuration, internal access check URL (pinged every five minutes), automatic upgrades and maintenance window.
Server prerequisites: supported Linux distribution, about 4 CPUs/4 GB/30 GB for small deployments, outbound TCP 443 (and 8090), Podman on RHEL or Docker elsewhere (rootless Podman supported).
Android Enterprise profile supports per-app and **Always-on** VPN; iOS profile supports per-app and **on-demand** rules (per-app VPN ignores split tunneling).

units.title: Extend support to MAM devices
points: Minimums: Android 10 (per-app or device-wide VPN), iOS 17 (per-app only).

Android needs three policies to the same groups: app config for Microsoft Defender (Use Microsoft Tunnel for MAM = Yes), app config for Edge (StrictTunnelMode, identity switching) and an Edge app protection policy with **Start Microsoft Tunnel connection on app-launch**.
Include Microsoft Edge in the Android per-app VPN list for identity switching.
iOS needs an app configuration policy, an app protection policy and, for private CAs, a trusted certificate profile (any platform's profile works).

units.title: Monitor and troubleshoot Tunnel connections
points: Health status shows Warning/Unhealthy metrics with configurable thresholds; the Trends tab averages data over three-hour blocks.
`mst-cli server status|restart|show`, `mst-cli agent restart`; logs via `journalctl -t ocserv`, `mstunnel-agent`, `mstunnel_monitor`.
Access logging is off by default: `TRACE_SESSIONS=1` (or 2 for DNS) in `/etc/mstunnel/env.sh`; it can reduce performance.
**Send logs** collects logs, enables verbosity level 4 for eight hours, uploads again and returns an Incident ID for Support.
Fixes: `/dev/net/tun` error → restart server; shows offline but works → reinstall; expiring TLS cert → `mst-cli import_cert` then restart.

keyTerms.definition: Containerized VPN service on Linux that connects mobile devices to on-premises resources.
Network settings (IP range, port, DNS, split tunneling) shared by all servers in a site.
Logical group of Tunnel servers sharing one public connection point and one server configuration.
Extends Tunnel to unenrolled Android and iOS/iPadOS devices using app-level policies.
Rules that route included IP ranges through the tunnel and send excluded ranges directly to the internet.
Command-line tool on the Tunnel server for status, restarts, connections and certificate import.

tables.title: Tunnel for enrolled vs unenrolled (MAM) devices
rows: Android: Defender app; iOS: Tunnel for MAM SDK in LOB apps
Android: per-app or Always-on; iOS: per-app or on-demand
Android: per-app or device-wide (no Always-on); iOS: per-app only

remember: BYOD phone needs on-prem access without enrollment → **Tunnel for MAM** (Plan 2 / Suite), same servers and sites.
Client IP range → **169.254.0.0/16**; split tunneling → never `0.0.0.0`.
Health shows offline but devices still connect → agent lost registration → **reinstall** Tunnel.
Tunnel for MAM on iOS → **per-app only**; on Android → **no Always-on**.

selfCheck.q: Devices fail to connect after the Linux host rebooted and the log shows `Can't open /dev/net/tun`. What do you do?
selfCheck.a: Run `sudo mst-cli server restart` (optionally automate with a cron job).

selfCheck.q: Which app do enrolled Android and iOS devices need to use Microsoft Tunnel?
selfCheck.a: The Microsoft Defender app, deployed from the store through Intune.

selfCheck.q: On unenrolled Android devices, what makes the tunnel start when Edge opens?
selfCheck.a: An Edge app protection policy with Start Microsoft Tunnel connection on app-launch set to Yes, alongside the Defender and Edge app configuration policies.

modules.title: Implement Microsoft Cloud PKI
modules.learnSummary: Stand up a cloud-hosted certificate authority hierarchy in Microsoft Intune, automate SCEP issuance and renewal, and monitor certificate health across managed devices.
